Linearity." editor: source format: revealjs: preview-links: true editor_options: chunk_output_type: console --- ::: {.cell} ::: --- #title: "t-test recap" editor: source format: revealjs: preview-links: true incremental: false editor_options: chunk_output_type: console --- # Example of an exam assignment The slides below show you what you can expect on an exam based on the material of the past weeks. Please note that: - these examples exaggerated the complexity of the exam. ## Definition question Answer **two** questions from the list below: - What measures of central tendency are most commonly applied in social sciences? - What are extreme observations or outliers? - What effect do outliers/extreme observations have on the mean/median, standard deviation/IQR? - Is the median one of the quantiles or is it a measure of central tendency? - What is the Hypothesis Testing? ## Problem introduction An RCT experiment was designed to understand the effect of technology ("Minimal" vs "Optimal") on rice yields. It included: 1. Randomly selecting 60 farms and offering them two equivalent rice varieties to plant. - each farmer picked one variety randomly. 2. Training half of them in applying Optimal technology (treatment), and 3. Keeping half of the farmers with the same minimal technology (control). During the production season, researchers recorded for each farm: - Technology, rice variety, rice yield, and fertilizer use. - The research objective was to measure the effect of technology on rice yield. Answer the questions on the following slides based on this example. ## Descriptive analysis (1) {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ::: ### Continuous variables ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

How does our sample ensure it? ::: ::: ::: ## Conclude again ::: incremental - Does the random assignment of technology ensure the ceteris paribus here? - What are the most relevant other factors that may influence the ceteris paribus in our sample? - Given that what can we conclude about the causal effect of technology on yields? - After today's lecture you should be able to answer the following: - Can we "control" the effects of the other factors? - What econometric method can we use to re-establish the ceteris paribus? - How (can we at all) measure the effects of other factors such as fertilizer application on the yields? ::: ## How to measure the effect of nitrogen fertilizer on yield? ::: {.cell} ::: ::: r-stack ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Framework for interpreting any statistical test {.smaller} ***For your reference and information.*** The keywords/concepts below are meant to improve the clarity of communication when performing the hypothesis testing. Please use it! They will help make your results understandable for the reader. 1. Test name and what it is about (t-test about means comparison between two groups). 2. $H_0$ and $H_1$. 3. Estimated parameters (means, coefficients, differences, standard error), $df$ / n observations. 4. Level of significance of the HT. ($\alpha = 0.05$ or 5% level of significance) 5. Rejection rule: $\text{p-value} < \alpha$ or $|t| < c_{df, \, 1 - \alpha /2}$ (statistics vs critical value) or $1 - \alpha$ confidence intervals (95% CI). 6. Conclusions: reject/fail to reject; 7. Implications - what do these conclusions imply for your analysis? - (for example. ... reject $H_0$. Thus, the mean "outcome" in the treatment group XX is higher than that in the control group, suggesting about the great success of our intervention ...). --- editor: source format: revealjs: preview-links: true editor_options: chunk_output_type: console --- # (Very) Simple Linear Regression two-variables linear or bi-variate linear regression model. > Explains how $y$ the Dependent variable > varies with > changes in $x$ the independent variable. ## SLR on population and sample {.smaller} ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ### Population regression (PRF) ::: fragment > Always unknown $$y = {\beta}_{0} + {\beta}_{1}x + u$$ - $y$ - dependent variable - $x$ - independent variable - ${\beta}_{0}$ - the true value of the intercept (constant term) - ${\beta}_{1}$ - the true value of the slope - $u$ - the true value of the error term or disturbance ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ### Estimated regression ::: fragment > What we learn from the sample of size $n$, where $i \in {1, 2, \dots, n}$ $$y_i = \hat{\beta}_{0} + \hat{\beta}_{1} x_i + \hat{u_i}$$ - $y_i$ - dependent variable from $i$ obs. in the sample - $x_i$ - independent variable - $\hat{\beta}_{0}$ - estimated intercept (constant term) - $\hat{\beta}_{1}$ - estimated slope\ - $\hat{u_i}$ - estimated error term or disturbance ::: ::: ::: ## Plot size and farmland prices ::: {.cell} ::: ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} We simulate a population of $2\times 10^{6}$ agricultural fields. Each field has only two characteristics: - price of 1 ha of land in in a land plot in Euro - size of a land plot in ha Each field could be different in quality of soil, landscape, accessibility but we assume that **the other things are equal**. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: footer See [@Ritter2020] for a discussion on the size-price relationship. ::: ## Regression Line ::: r-stack ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Regression Line (cont.) ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: r-stack ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-26-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: fragment `plot_large` is a dummy variable also called an "indicator variable" ::: ::: r-stack ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 600 × 4 area value plot_size plot_large 1 3.79 3180. Large plot 1 2 3.01 2920. Large plot 1 3 1.10 1252. Small plot 0 4 1.06 1669. Small plot 0 5 2.23 2656. Small plot 0 6 4.11 3276. Large plot 1 7 3.65 4393. Large plot 1 8 0.705 928. Small plot 0 # ℹ 588 more rows ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-28-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-29-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-30-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-31-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Regression Line (cont.) ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-32-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} t.test(value ~ plot_size, plot_pop_dta2) # Welch Two Sample t-test # data: value by plot_size # t = -29.887, df = 594.75, p-value < 2.2e-16 # alternative hypothesis: true difference in means # between group Small plot and group Large plot # is not equal to 0 # 95 percent confidence interval: # -2094.443 -1836.148 # sample estimates: # mean in group Small plot # 1699.595 # mean in group Large plot # 3664.890 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Regression: Coefficients Regression parameters / coefficient ($\hat{\beta}_0$ and $\hat{\beta}_1$) are estimated using the [Ordinary Least Squares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinary_least_squares) (OLS) method. These are: ::: fragment **The intercept**: ($\hat{\beta}_0$) - is the value of $\hat{y}$, when all regressors ($x$) are zero. ::: ::: fragment **The slope**: ($\hat{\beta}_1$) - change in the **expected value of** $\hat{y}$ (in units of $y$), when $x$ **increases by one unit**. ::: ## Regression: Coefficients interpretation ::: columns ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell fig-heigts='6'} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-34-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="60%"} In the example of land price, where $\hat{\beta_0} = 656.15$ and $\hat{\beta_1} = 810.95$: ::: fragment Intercept: - On average, starting price of a land plot with near to zero size is 656.15 Euros per ha. ::: ::: fragment Slope: - The **expected price of 1 ha of land** increases by 810.95 Euros when the plot size increases by 1 HA ::: ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ## Regression: OLS Algorithm {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ::: ::: columns ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: r-stack ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-37-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: {.fragment fragment-index="1"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-38-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment fragment-index="2"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-39-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment fragment-index="3"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-40-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.fragment fragment-index="1"} 1 Proposes $\hat{\beta_0}$ and $\hat{\beta_1}$ so that actual values are: $y_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \cdot x_i + \hat{u}_i$ ::: ::: {.fragment fragment-index="2"} 2 Computes **fitted values** ($\hat{y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \cdot x_i$) and **residuals** ($\hat{u}_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i$). ::: ::: {.fragment fragment-index="4"} 3 Computes **squared residuals** and the sum of it $\sum \hat{u}^2$ ::: ::: {.fragment fragment-index="5"} 4 Repeats 1-3 with new estimates of $\hat{\beta_0}$ and $\hat{\beta_1}$; ::: ::: {.fragment fragment-index="5"} 5 Compare new **sum of squared residuals** $\sum \hat{u}$ to the previous one. ::: ::: {.fragment fragment-index="6"} 6 Repeats 4-5 to minimize **sum of squared residuals** until it no longer reduces. ::: ::: {.fragment fragment-index="7"} 7 Estimates of $\hat{\beta_0} = 656.15$ and $\hat{\beta_1} = 810.95$ are values, where sum of squared residuals are minimal ($\sum \hat{u}^2 = 530,480,825,704.7$). ::: ::: ::: ## Population Regression Function and Random sampling ::: incremental - **we never have the entire population** - instead, **we can only derive (random) samples** - Therefore, absolute estimates of the population's parameters (slope and intercept) are insufficient. - We need to perform ... - Hypothesis testing! ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: fragment To illustrate this, let us follow-up on the simulated population and derive **6 random samples** of **9 observations** in each sample. ::: ## Sample variation {.smaller} **population regression line is in red** and **estimated regression line is in blue** ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-42-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ## Regression: Inference {.smaller} ::: columns ::: {.column width="70%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="4-6,10"} fit0 <- lm(value ~ area, land_pop) summary(fit0) #> Coefficients: #> Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) #> (Intercept) 656.4388 0.7503 874.9 <2e-16 *** #> area 810.8136 0.2574 3150.0 <2e-16 *** #> --- #> Signif. codes: 0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1 #> #> Residual standard error: 515 on 1999998 degrees of freedom #> Multiple R-squared: 0.8322, Adjusted R-squared: 0.8322 #> F-statistic: 9.922e+06 on 1 and 1999998 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="30%"} $H_0:\beta = 0$ $H_1:\beta \neq 0$ ::: fragment $t = {\hat{\beta}}/{se_{\hat\beta}}$ ::: ::: fragment $t^* = c_{df, \, 1 - \alpha /2}$ ::: ::: ::: ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: fragment $df = n - k$ with $n$ number of observations and $k$ number of regressors $k = 2$ (one for the intercept and one the slope). ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: fragment - Reject $H_0$, when - $|t| > t^*$, or - $\text{p-value} < 0.05$, or - ${\hat{\beta}}/{se_{\hat\beta}} > 2$ (rule of thumb). - Fail to reject $H_0$ otherwise. ::: ::: ::: ## Regression: Goodness of Fit {.smaller} ::: columns ::: {.column width="70%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="11"} fit0 <- lm(value ~ area, land_pop) summary(fit0) #> Coefficients: #> Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) #> (Intercept) 656.4388 0.7503 874.9 <2e-16 *** #> area 810.8136 0.2574 3150.0 <2e-16 *** #> --- #> Signif. codes: 0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1 #> #> Residual standard error: 515 on 1999998 degrees of freedom #> Multiple R-squared: 0.8322, Adjusted R-squared: 0.8322 #> F-statistic: 9.922e+06 on 1 and 1999998 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="30%"} Explanatory power of the model: - R-squared ::: ::: ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: fragment R-squared: measures the fraction of variance in the dependent variable that is explained by the independent variable. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: fragment Adjusted R-squared: accounts for the number of independent variables, usually decreasing compared to the R-squared, when we add irrelevant independent variables. ::: ::: ::: ## Key Takaway concepts - Regression coefficients: an intercept and a slope - Interpretation of the regression coefficients - Statistical inference about the regression coefficients - Fitted (predicted) values - Error terms - Adjusted R squared. # Self-study: Simple Linear Regression Examples Review examples below at home: - Discuss how would you interpret the coefficients? ## Example 1 {.smaller} ![](img/ex1-slr-pic-1.png){width="100%"} ::: incremental Comment on (1) what relationship is measured by this regression? (2) what are the interpretations of the coefficients? - $\beta_0$ indicates the **expected level** of $yield$ (in the units of $yield$ ) given **zero** level of $fertilizer$ application given that other things (rainfall, land quality, etc.) - $\beta_1$ indicates the **expected change** in $yield$ (in the units of $yield$ ) given **one unit change** (usually increase, but not always) in $fertilizer$ application given that other factors remain fixed (rainfall, land quality, etc.) ::: ::: footer Source: [@wooldridge2020introductory] ::: ## Example 2 ![](img/ex1-slr-pic-2.png){width="100%"} ::: incremental Interpret the slope: - With the one year increase in education, average hourly wage increases / (decreases) by $\beta_1$. ::: ## Example 3 Ozone $O^3$ in stratosphere {.smaller} The goal of this example is to show that simple linear regression could be used for exposing trends and showing how those trends change significantly after the introduction of a new policy. ::: incremental - Ozone $O^3$ - forms in the stratosphere from oxygen under influence of ultraviolet radiation; - The amount of ozone in the atmosphere is very small; - Ozone absorbs most of the ultraviolet radiation from the sun; - Ozone holes expose humanity to solar radiation. ::: ## Background {.smaller} ::: incremental - In 1971, [James Lovelock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lovelock) had discovered a new compound in the earth's atmosphere, trichlorofluoromethane, a chlorofluorocarbon (CFC). See: [@Lovelock1971] - In 1974 [Sherwood Rowland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F._Sherwood_Rowland) and [Mario Molina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Molina) [@Molina1974] discovered the mechanism how CFC gases damage the ozone layer by photolysis. (In 1995 together with [Paul Crutzen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_J._Crutzen) they were awarded a 1995 Nobel Prize in Chemistry) - In 1987, [The Montreal Protocol](https://www.unep.org/ozonaction/who-we-are/about-montreal-protocol) was accepted by 191 countries aiming to reduce the levels of ozone depleting substances (ODSs) in the atmosphere. - It took humanity only 14 years to bridge scientific finding with the global policy. ::: ::: footer Data source: [gml.noaa.gov](https://gml.noaa.gov/aftp/data/hats/cfcs/cfc11/combined/HATS_global_F11.txt) ::: ## The problem: Let us establish a causal effect between the Montreal Protocol and the global CFC-11 emissions/concentration. ## CFC-11 content in the atmosphere ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-46-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ## To establish a causal relationship, ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} we can: ::: incremental - split data into **Before** and **After** The Montreal Protocol; - fit two separate simple regressions: $\text{CFC-11} = \hat \beta_0 + \hat \beta_1 \cdot \text{year} + \hat u$ ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ### Why Ceteris Paribus is satisfied here? ::: fragment ::: incremental - There are no other factors which could have affected the CFC-11 emissions but the Montreal Protocol. - Technology change, although endogenous, has forced to reduce CFC-11 emissions due to the Protocol. ::: ::: ::: ::: ## CFC-11 content over time (Monthly averages) ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-47-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ## Results of the SLR (1): Coefficients values ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-48-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ## Results of the simple regression (2) ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-49-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: # Multiple regression - Watch: Selection Bias: - Readings for your reference: - Chapter 2 in @Angrist2014 - Chapter 3 in @Angrist2009 --- editor: source format: revealjs: preview-links: true editor_options: chunk_output_type: console --- ## Multiple Linear Regression vocabulary Regression equation: $$y = \hat {\beta}_{0} + \hat {\beta}_{1}x_1 + \hat {\beta}_{2}x_2 + \hat {\beta}_{3}x_3 + \cdots + \hat {\beta}_{k}x_k + \hat u$$ ::: incremental - $y$ the dependent variable; - $x_1, x_2, x_3, \cdots x_k$ the independent variables from the set $k$; - $\hat {\beta}_{0}$ - intercept (constant term); - $\hat {\beta}_{1}$, $\hat {\beta}_{2}$, $\hat {\beta}_{k}$ - coefficients / parameters associated with $x_1$, $x_2$, ... $x_k$; ::: ## Multiple Linear Regression vocabulary (cont.) After we estimate the regression equation and obtain our estimates $\hat {\beta}_{0}, \hat {\beta}_{1}, \hat {\beta}_{2}, \cdots, \hat {\beta}_{k}$ we can calculate: ::: fragment $\hat y$ fitted of predicted value or the dependent variable and $\hat u$ error terms ::: ::: fragment $$\hat y = \hat {\beta}_{0} + \hat {\beta}_{1}x_1 + \hat {\beta}_{2}x_2 + \hat {\beta}_{3}x_3 + \cdots + \hat {\beta}_{k}x_k$$ ::: ::: fragment $$\hat u = y - \hat y$$ ::: ## Motivation befind MLR ::: incremental - To incorporate more explanatory factors into a model; - Explicitly hold fixed (some) other factors; - Allow for more flexible functional forms; - To correct the selection bias problem in the absence of (poor quality of) the RCT; - To establish the ceteris paribus in observational data; ::: ## Interpretation - The multiple linear regression shows the effect of each variable, holding other explanatory variables fixed; ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-51-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: fragment ::: callout-important ### We assume that all unobserved factors do not change if the explanatory variables are changed. ::: ::: ## Example 1. Wage equation ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-52-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ## Example 2. Average test scores and spending ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-53-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ## Example 3. CEO salary, sales and CEO tenure ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-54-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: incremental - Model assumes a constant elasticity relationship between CEO salary and the sales of his or her firm. - Model assumes a quadratic relationship between CEO salary and his or her tenure with the firm. ::: ## Mechanics $$y = \hat {\beta}_{0} + \hat {\beta}_{1}x_1 + \hat {\beta}_{2}x_2 + \hat {\beta}_{3}x_3 + \cdots + \hat {\beta}_{k}x_k + \hat u$$ ::: incremental 1. MLR uses the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) method to **estimate regression parameters** $\beta$. - Such parameters $\beta$ are found that the sum of squared errors is minimal. 2. As any estimate of $\beta$ is based on a sample, we need to relay on the **inference** to test a hypothesis about the true coefficients in the population. ::: # Example MLR (1). Effect of fuel taxes on petrol consumption We use data on motor fuel consumption and related variables, for the year 2001. Each observation represents a state in the United States. (based on the data from @weisberg2005a). Variables are: - $Tax$ : Gasoline state tax rate, cents per liter - $Dlic$ : The number of licensed drivers per 1000 population over the age of 16; - $Income$ : in 1000 USD Per capita personal income (year 2000) - $Miles$ : Miles of Federal-aid highway miles in the state - $Fuel$ : Gasoline consumption per capita (liter) ## 1. Problem formulation {.smaller} How do fuel taxes affect gasoline consumption?: ::: fragment ### 2. Regression model and hypothesis Write a regression equation: ::: fragment $$Fuel = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 Tax + \hat\beta_2 Dlic + \hat\beta_3 Income + \hat\beta_4 Miles + \hat{u}$$ ::: Discuss, what effects can we expect from change in each variable $x$ on $y$? ::: fragment Hypotheses: - $\hat\beta_0$ [$>0$ because on average some consumption should occur]{.fragment} - $\hat\beta_1$ [$<0$ taxes make flue more expensive leading people to consume less]{.fragment} - $\hat\beta_2$ [$>0$ more people with driving licences increase consumption of flue]{.fragment} - $\hat\beta_3$ [$>0$ higher income relaxes budget constraints allowing to drive more]{.fragment} - $\hat\beta_4$ [$>0$ a larger road network makes people drive more]{.fragment} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ## Exploratory data analysis (1) {.smaller} ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} |rowname | mean| sd| median| skew| kurtosis| se| |:--------|------:|-----:|------:|-----:|--------:|-----:| |Tax | 20.15| 4.54| 20.00| -0.67| 0.55| 0.64| |Dlic | 903.68| 72.86| 909.07| -0.30| 0.31| 10.20| |Income | 28.40| 4.45| 27.87| 0.62| -0.04| 0.62| |logMiles | 10.91| 1.03| 11.28| -1.43| 1.92| 0.14| |Fuel | 613.13| 88.96| 626.02| -0.88| 2.09| 12.46| ::: ::: ::: fragment **Variable of interest:** `Tax`. **Outcome variable:** `Fule`. ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} ### What kind of relationship exists between Tax and Fuel? ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-57-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Exploratory data analysis (2) ### What kind of relationship exists between Tax and Fuel? ::: r-stack ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-58-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-59-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## 4. Estimating a Simple Linear Reg. {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="1,2,5-8"} fit_fule_0 <- lm(Fuel ~ Tax, fule_cons) summary(fit_fule_0) # Coefficients: # Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) # (Intercept) 715.485 55.770 12.829 <2e-16 *** # Tax -5.078 2.701 -1.881 0.066 . ``` ::: ### What does it show? ::: incremental - The estaimted effect of taxes is -5.1. - A unit change in tax level (1 cent increase in taxes per liter) - **reduces** fuel consumption by 5.1 liters per person - assuming all other factors are fixed. - However, p-value \> 0.05. The same effect of taxes may not hold for the population. - Is this the true **causal effect**? Is there the Ceteris Paribus? - NO! We do not control for other things! ::: ## 4. Estimating the Multiple Linear Regression {.smaller} Multiple linear regression helps to reveal the true causal effect of `Tax` by - controlling all other things - making them equal when the tax changes by one unit ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="1,2,5-6,8-9"} fit_fule_1 <- lm(Fuel ~ Tax + Dlic + Income + logMiles, fule_cons) summary(fit_fule_1) # Coefficients: # Estimate Std. Inspecting and interpreting the results Here we need to: - perform the HT about estimated coefficients; - interpretation of their economic meaning; - compare estimates with ex-ante expectations. ## The Intercept {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="1,2,5"} fit_fule_1 <- lm(Fuel ~ Tax + Dlic + Income + logMiles, fule_cons) summary(fit_fule_1) # Coefficients: # Estimate Std. (p-value = 0.432). - Contradicts our ex-ante hypothesis about some basic level of fuel consumption; - Suggests that the absence of a road network could drive fuel consumption to zero. ::: ## The Slope of Taxes {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="1,2,6"} fit_fule_1 <- lm(Fuel ~ Tax + Dlic + Income + logMiles, fule_cons) summary(fit_fule_1) # Coefficients: # Estimate Std. Var. | Indep. Var. | Interpretation of $\beta_1$ | Interpretation | |:-------------:|:-------------:|:-------------:|:-------------:|:-------------:| | Level-level | $y$ | $x$ | $\Delta y = \beta_1 \Delta x$ | 1 unit change in $x$ causes $\beta_1$ units change in $y$ | | Level-log | $y$ | $log(x)$ | $\Delta y = (\beta_1/100)\% \Delta x$ | 1 % change in $x$ causes $\beta_1/100$ units change in $y$ | | Log-level | $log(y)$ | $x$ | $\% \Delta y = (100\beta_1) \Delta x$ | 1 unit change in $x$ causes $100 \beta_1$ % change in $y$ | | Log-log | $log(y)$ | $log(x)$ | $\% \Delta y = \beta_1 \% \Delta x$ | 1 % change in $x$ causes $\beta_1$ % change in $y$ (elasticity) | - Power transformation ($x^2$, $\sqrt x$), Box-Cox transformations; - Variables normalization to the standard normal distribution; - Tailor expansion (Cobb-Douglas, Trans-log) # Linearity Example 1: Anscombe quartet ## The Anscombe quartet {.smaller} - Four data sets of 11 observations each and two variables (x and y). ::: columns ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: fragment ### SLR y on x ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Scatter plots ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-114-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ## Residuals vs fitted ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](mk68-06-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-116-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: # Takeaways checklist ## Key concepts covered in the lecture {.smaller} ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} Simple linear regression: - Regressor and regressand; - Fitted values and residuals; - OLS method; - Estimated coefficients; - Interpretation of the slope and the intercept. - HT about the regression coefficients. Ceteris Paribus - Establishing Ceteris Paribus without an RCT. - Multiple Linear Regression that controls for other things. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} Multiple linear regression - Coefficients, HT and interpretation. - Goodness of fit. - Causal meaning. - Observed included, not included and unobserved factors. - Interpreting coefficients of the MLR. Assumptions of the regression analysis. - Bias and unbiased estimates. - Role of assumptions in the bias of the estimates. Linearity assumption - Detection. - Implications or why the linearity assumption is important. - How to correct the non-linearity (linear transformation). ::: ::: # Self-study: Cradle of the Regression Analysis - The term "regression" was coined by Sir Francis Galton, Charles Darwin's half-cousin, in 1886 - he was gripped by Darwin's masterpiece, The Origin of Species. - he used "Regression" to prove his points of Eugenics... > Statistics has some dark history... > Paper: Francis Galton, "Regression towards Mediocrity in Hereditary Stature," Journal of the Anthropological Institute of Great Britain and Ireland, vol. 15, 1886, pages 246--263 ## Galton's introduction of regression - Galton discovered that the average heights of fathers and sons are linked by a regression equation. - the average height of sons is a weighted average of their fathers' height and the average height in the population from which the fathers and sons were sampled. ## First application in causality analysis - pioneered by George Udny Yule in "An Investigation into the Causes of Changes in Pauperism in England, Chiefly during the Last Two Intercensal Decades," Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, vol. 62, no. 2, June 1899, pages 249--295. - Student of statistician Karl Pearson (Pearson's correlation ...) and Galton's protege. Yule realized that Galton's regression method could be extended to include many variables (multiple regression). ## George Udny Yule {.smaller} In an 1899 MLR was used to link the administration of the English Poor Laws in different counties to the likelihood county residents were poor, while controlling for population growth and the age distribution in the county. - The poor laws provided subsistence for the indigent, usually by offering shelter and employment in institutions called workhouses. - Yule was particularly interested in whether the practice of outdoor relief, which provided income support for poor people without requiring them to move to a workhouse, increased poverty rates by making pauperism less onerous. - This is a well-defined causal question much like those that occupy social scientists today. ## The past of statistics Statistics has a dark past. - It was used and developed in the disposal of really terrible things like Eugenics. - But the world was terrible then. Nowadays, same statistical methods are fundamental for revealing causal effects as 100 years ago. - Yet we apply it for some different causes. # References
